blocks.text: On 29 May 1999 a Nigerian general handed the presidency to an elected civilian, ending sixteen years of military rule. Nothing had been discovered and no war had been won. A queue of ordinary voters had simply been allowed to decide — and that is the whole idea of democracy.

blocks.markdown:
The word **democracy** comes from the Greek *demos*, meaning the people, and *kratia*, meaning rule. Abraham Lincoln's definition in the Gettysburg Address of 1863 remains the most quoted: government **of** the people, **by** the people and **for** the people.

More precisely, democracy is a system in which supreme power rests with the people, who exercise it either directly or through freely elected representatives, under rules that protect the rights of those who lose.

blocks.title: Direct and indirect democracy
blocks.text: In a DIRECT or pure democracy the citizens themselves assemble to make laws and decide policy, as in the city-state of ancient Athens and in some Swiss cantons. In an INDIRECT or representative democracy the citizens elect representatives to make those decisions on their behalf, which is what Nigeria, Ghana, the United States and India practise. Direct democracy survives in modern states mainly through devices such as the referendum, the plebiscite, the initiative and the recall.

blocks.markdown:
### Principles of democracy

These are the tests an examiner expects you to apply to any claim that a country is democratic.

items: **Popular sovereignty** — ultimate authority belongs to the people.
**Universal adult suffrage** — every qualified adult has one vote of equal value; the voting age in Nigeria is 18.
**Periodic free and fair elections** — power is contested at regular, constitutionally fixed intervals.
**Majority rule with minority rights** — the majority governs, but the minority keeps its rights to speak, organise and try again.
**Rule of law and constitutionalism** — government itself is bound by law.
**Fundamental human rights** — guaranteed and enforceable in the courts.
**Separation of powers and an independent judiciary** — so that no single organ becomes unanswerable.
**Freedom of the press and of association** — citizens must be able to inform themselves and to organise.
**Political accountability** — officeholders must explain and answer for their conduct.

rows: Government is accountable, since voters can dismiss it at the next election
Decision making is slow because of debate, committees and consultation
Peaceful and orderly change of government reduces coups and violence
Elections and legislatures are expensive to run
Fundamental rights and the rule of law are protected
Voters may be poorly informed, so campaigns can be won by propaganda
Citizens participate and receive political education
The majority can oppress a minority — the tyranny of the majority
Minority views can be expressed and can eventually prevail
Money politics and godfatherism can put wealth ahead of merit
Power is dispersed, so tyranny is harder to establish
Politicians may prefer popular short-term measures to necessary hard ones
blocks.caption: A balanced evaluation of democracy — use both columns in essay answers

blocks.title: Planning an essay: "Is a country with regular elections necessarily democratic?"
blocks.prompt: Build a structured answer to this question in five moves.

steps.text: Define the key terms. Democracy is rule by the people through freely elected representatives, resting on more than the holding of elections alone.
Concede the point in favour. Regular elections satisfy the principles of popular sovereignty, periodic contest and accountability, so they are a necessary condition.

Show why they are not sufficient. An election can be held while opposition candidates are jailed, results are falsified, the judiciary is controlled, or the press is muzzled. The form of democracy is then present without its substance.
Supply the test. Ask whether the other principles hold: universal suffrage, free and fair conduct, rule of law, protected rights, independent courts and a free press.

Conclude firmly. Elections are necessary but not sufficient; democracy requires the full set of principles, so a country with elections alone is better described as an electoral facade than a democracy.

blocks.answer: No. Regular elections are a necessary but not a sufficient condition; democracy also requires free and fair conduct, rule of law, protected rights, an independent judiciary and a free press.

blocks.title: Quote precisely
blocks.text: If you use Lincoln's definition, give it exactly — "government of the people, by the people, for the people" — and then explain each phrase: of means the people are the source of authority, by means they participate in choosing rulers, for means government must serve their interest. Explaining the phrase earns more than merely quoting it.

points: Democracy is rule by the people, exercised directly or through elected representatives.
Direct democracy operated in ancient Athens; modern states use representative democracy with devices such as the referendum.
Its principles include popular sovereignty, universal adult suffrage, periodic free elections, majority rule with minority rights and the rule of law.
Its merits include accountability, peaceful change of government and protection of rights.
Its demerits include slow and costly decision making, money politics and the risk of majority tyranny.
Elections alone do not make a democracy; the other principles must hold as well.
